entries.name: Open-pit mine
entries.era: prehistoric to now (large-scale since the 19th century)
entries.purpose: cheapest way to reach shallow, low-grade ore (porphyry copper, gold, iron, coal)
parts: benches in terraces 16-25 m high
spiral haul roads from rim to pit floor
grid drill pattern for blasting
waste-rock dumps around the rim
in-pit crusher and conveyor
tailings pond or dump
layout: pit deepens by pushing benches back in sequence
roads spiral down the final pit wall
waste and ore separated at the shovel
entries.found: wherever ore outcrops or lies near the surface: most of the world's copper, iron and coal
entries.notes: Numbers are typical, not fixed: pits range from a few hectares to 4 km across. Terraced benches are the signature silhouette at any distance.

entries.name: Strip mine
entries.purpose: recover flat-lying coal and lignite seams by removing the overburden in strips
parts: parallel strips with spoil cast into the previous strip
dragline or shovel fleets
overburden casts and reclaimed benches
coal handling plant and rail loading
layout: strips run parallel to the outcrop
overburden from strip N fills strip N-1
reclaiming the land trails just behind the mining face
entries.found: flat coalfields: Powder River Basin (Wyoming), Rhineland (Germany), Latrobe Valley (Australia)
entries.notes: Powder River Basin mines move on the order of 100 Mt of coal a year and are reclaimed to farmland or grass as they advance.

entries.name: Mountaintop removal mine
entries.purpose: extract buried Appalachian coal seams by blasting off ridge tops
parts: ridge-top blasting benches
valley fills of overburden burying headwater streams
haul roads and sediment ponds
reclaimed grass or shrub flats where forest used to be
layout: seam followed along the ridge crest
valleys filled with the displaced rock
spectacular flat-topped mesas left where rounded forested ridges were
entries.found: central Appalachia (West Virginia, Kentucky, Virginia), USA; banned or restricted elsewhere
entries.notes: Among the most destructive surface mining: valley fills bury streams and the flat barren benches persist for decades.

entries.name: Placer mine
entries.purpose: wash gold (and tin, diamonds, gemstones) out of stream gravels
parts: excavation of gravel bars and ancient terraces
sluice boxes with riffles and carpet
water supply from ditches or pumps
tailing piles of washed gravel
layout: gravel worked in stretches along the creek
water diverted through the sluice
gold settles behind the riffles
entries.found: gold districts worldwide; the California Gold Rush (1848-1855) was placer mining
entries.notes: The original gold-rush image: pans and rockers. Modern placer operations move gravel with excavators into washing plants.

entries.name: Gold dredge
entries.purpose: excavate gold-bearing gravel mechanically from river valleys and offshore bars
parts: bucket-line ladder at the bow
revolving screen (trommel) and sluice riffles inside
stacker conveyor casting tailings astern
dredge pond dug by the dredge itself
layout: dredge floats in its own pond and eats the bank ahead of it
tailings stacked behind in long sinuous ridges
pond and ridge tailings remain as a signature landscape
entries.found: Klondike (Canada), Yuba Goldfields (California), New Zealand, Russia, offshore Nome (Alaska)
entries.notes: Bucket dredges carved the long pitted gravel ridges you still see along auriferous river valleys; several are preserved as museums.

entries.name: Drift (adit) mine
entries.purpose: horizontal-entry working at valley level, draining by gravity
parts: horizontal portal in the hillside
drifts along the ore
crosscuts, raises and winzes
adit or tunnel exit downhill for drainage
layout: single horizontal entrance partway up the slope
workings follow the orebody into the hill
water drains out through the portal
entries.found: mountainous ore districts; Roman Las Médulas (Spain) was the greatest of all
entries.notes: Las Médulas was worked by hydraulic hushing: entire hillsides washed away to expose gold, leaving the spectacular red pinnacle landscape.

entries.name: Aggregate quarry
entries.purpose: supply concrete, road base and asphalt: the largest volume of any mining on Earth
parts: bench faces in rock or gravel banks
crushing and screening plant
washing ponds and sumps
stockpile ridges by grade
layout: low wide pit with several working benches
plant sits at the pit floor or adjacent
truck or rail loading yard at the gate
entries.found: near every city; most concrete in the world contains this stone
entries.notes: Concrete is the most used human material after water; aggregate quarries out-punch every metal mine combined by mass.

entries.name: Dimension stone quarry
entries.purpose: cut building and monumental stone to exact block dimensions
parts: vertical cutting faces with wire-saw kerfs
benches parted by channel cuts or wedge lines
block yards and sawing sheds
water or slurry management
layout: benches developed to extract whole blocks
blocks walked to the yard by crane or rail
waste fines and sludge heaps nearby
entries.found: wherever durable stone crops out: Carrara (Italy), Rajasthan (India), Vermont (USA), Xiamen (China)
entries.notes: Quality is judged by sawing flawlessness: one cracked block writes off the whole face.

entries.name: Mine headframe
entries.purpose: the visible tower over a shaft: hoists cage and skip, signals, ventilation
parts: A-frame or four-post tower
head sheave at the summit
winding engine house adjacent (older) or hidden drive (modern)
skip dump at the top into the tipple
cage landing and waiting room
layout: shaft drops vertical below the tower
winding rope runs over the sheave to the engine house
ore dumps at the top into a tipple feeding rail or truck
entries.found: every shaft mine; Cornish beam-engine houses are the romantic ruin version
entries.notes: Cornish engine houses (18th-19th c.) pumped water out of tin and copper mines and exported the design worldwide; their ruins still punctuate the Cornish coast.

entries.name: Spoil tip (colliery waste heap)
entries.purpose: dump the rock that separates the ore from nothing
parts: conical or ridged waste pile
occasional burning (smouldering tips)
reclaimed grass or pioneer vegetation
layout: tip grows beside the pit or shaft
rail-fed tips form long ridges; dragline tips form cones
entries.found: coal and metal mining districts; the Ruhr, South Wales, northern France, Appalachia
entries.notes: Aberfan (Wales, 21 October 1966): a rain-saturated coal-waste tip slid onto a school, killing 116 children and 28 adults; it remains the defining spoil-tip disaster.

entries.name: Bingham Canyon Mine (Kennecott)
entries.purpose: the largest man-made excavation on Earth; porphyry copper with gold and silver
parts: terraced benches 16-25 m high
spiral haul roads to a pit floor 1.2 km down
in-pit crusher and 8 km conveyor to the concentrator
tailings ponds and smelter at Copperton
layout: 4 km wide, 1.2 km deep, ~7.7 km2 surface
benches retreat as mining deepens
2013 landslide removed ~65-70 million m3 without casualties (evacuation worked)
entries.found: Oquirrh Mountains, 30 km southwest of Salt Lake City, Utah, USA
entries.notes: Produces on the order of 17 Mt Cu so far plus molybdenum, gold, silver; visible from space; still deepening toward a planned limit ~200 m lower.

entries.name: Chuquicamata
entries.era: 1910 to now (open pit to 2019, underground block caving since)
entries.purpose: bulk porphyry copper-moly mining; once the world's largest annual copper producer
parts: open pit ~4.5 km by 3.0 km, about 1 km deep
smelter and electrolytic refinery on site
worker camp closed 2007, now a ghost town with guided tours
underground block-caving macroblocks below the pit
layout: pit sits at 2,850 m a.s.l. in the Atacama
ore hauled up ramps, smelted beside the pit
pre-Columbian 'Chucos' worked the surface oxidised ores first
entries.found: 16 km north of Calama, Antofagasta Region, Chile
entries.notes: About 29 Mt Cu produced overall, the largest total from any copper mine; nationalized by Chile in 1971 (Codelco); open pit ended 2019 as the economics flipped to caving.

entries.name: Escondida
entries.purpose: the world's largest copper producer
parts: two open pits feeding three concentrators
oxide leach heaps and cathode plants
220 km pipeline pumping desalinated seawater up to 3,100 m
worker camps on site
layout: pits at ~3,100 m in the hyper-arid Atacama
concentrate trucked ~170 km to port at Antofagasta
operates largely on renewable power purchased from the grid
entries.found: Antofagasta Region, Chile
entries.notes: Around 1.3 Mt Cu per year recently (~6% of world mine production). Exact pit dimensions not published as a single figure; the site is the benchmark for giant copper.

entries.name: Grasberg mine
entries.era: 1990 to now (open pit 1990-2019, block caving since)
entries.purpose: world's largest gold mine and a top copper producer
parts: depleted open pit at 4,285 m a.s.l.
underground block caves: Grasberg Block Cave, DMLZ, Big Gossan
ore column 1.8 km deep in the Grasberg Igneous Complex
term-of-art mine camp at Tembagapura
layout: at the headwaters of the Ajkwa River in the Sudirman Range
ore body: ~2 billion tonnes at ~1% Cu and ~1 g/t Au
27 billion lb Cu and 46 million oz Au produced 1990-2019 from the open pit alone
entries.found: highlands of Papua (formerly Irian Jaya), near Carstensz Pyramid, Indonesia
entries.notes: One of the most remote large mines on Earth; environmental legacy of the Ajkwa tailings river is contested; open pit ceased 2019, underground continues.

entries.name: Kalgoorlie Super Pit (Fimiston)
entries.purpose: Australia's largest open-cut gold mine
parts: rectangular pit ~3.5 km by 1.5 km, ~600 m deep
amalgam of 260+ original small mines (KCGM, 1989)
Mt Charlotte underground mine adjacent
layout: Golden Mile reef belt followed 3.5 km along strike
3,500 km of old underground workings swallowed by the pit
visible from space; tourist lookout on the rim
entries.found: Kalgoorlie-Boulder, Western Australia
entries.notes: ~65 million oz gold since 1893; founded on Paddy Hannan's 1893 discovery; forecast expansion to ~4 km by 2032.

entries.name: Hull-Rust-Mahoning Mine (Mesabi Range)
entries.purpose: iron ore for US steel: the largest open-pit iron mine in the world
parts: pit over 5 km long, up to 2.4 km wide, 163 m deep
world's first large mechanized open-pit operations (1892-95)
observation platform for visitors
taconite pellet plants at Hibbing and Virginia
layout: Mesabi monocline dipping gently southeast
ore railed to Duluth docks and loaded onto Great Lakes freighters
town of Hibbing sits beside the pit; parts of it were relocated for expansion
entries.found: Hibbing, Minnesota, USA
entries.notes: Roughly 1 billion tons of ore shipped; supplied about a quarter of US iron ore through both world wars; Michigan iron fueled the US steel boom.

entries.name: The Big Hole (Kimberley Mine)
entries.purpose: the largest hand-dug excavation in the world; the diamond rush that created De Beers
parts: round pit 463 m across, 17 ha surface, 1.6 km perimeter
22.5 Mt of earth removed by ~50,000 diggers
underground mine reached 1,097 m below
open-air museum with 1880s recreated town
layout: colesberg kopje flattened entirely
claims laid out in a regular grid of 31-ft squares
exchange and De Beers consolidation ended the free dig
entries.found: Kimberley, Northern Cape, South Africa
entries.notes: Yielded ~2,722 kg of diamonds (13.6M carats). Excavated to 240 m, then partially refilled; about 40 m of water now hides the bottom.

entries.name: Mir mine
entries.purpose: USSR's first and largest diamond mine; the Yakutian diamond boom
parts: conical pit 1.2 km diameter, 525 m deep
Metegero-Ichersky aquifer beneath the permafrost flooded the pit bottom
underground block-caving beneath the flooded pit (2009-2017)
layout: permafrost let the pit hold near-vertical walls
mir = 'peace', the Soviet answer to De Beers
helicopters are forbidden to fly over the pit (downdraft)
entries.found: Mirny, Sakha Republic, Russia (62.5 N)
entries.notes: Produced over 200 million carats; the pit is the 4th deepest in the world; visible on satellite imagery; the town of Mirny (pop. ~35,000) exists only because of the mine.

entries.name: Kiruna mine
materials: magnetite ore in an 80-120 m thick, 4 km long sheet
entries.purpose: world's largest underground iron-ore mine
parts: ore body 4 km long, 80-120 m thick, dips 60 degrees east
main haulage level at 1,365 m below the outcrop
sub-level caving from the 1960s
concentrating and pelletising plants at site
layout: mining proceeds top-down; the hanging wall collapses behind
subsidence cracks reached the town; the entire city centre is moving 3 km east (since 2014, to 2040)
Kiruna Church was jacked onto trailers and driven to the new site in August 2025
entries.found: Kiruna, Norrbotten, Swedish Lapland
entries.notes: Over 950 Mt ore produced since 1898; about 27 Mt per year; exports by rail over the Arctic mountains to the ice-free port of Narvik.

entries.name: Big Pit (Blaenavon)
entries.purpose: Deep-screen coal for Welsh industry; now the UK's national coal museum
parts: 90 m (300 ft) shaft descended by cage
colliery buildings: winding engine house, pithead baths, lamp room, stables
working faces and stables on the 300 ft level
Blaenavon Industrial Landscape World Heritage Site (2000)
layout: cage drops 90 m in ~30 seconds
underground tour follows 50-minute walk by a former miner guide
peak ~1,300 men, ~250,000 t coal a year
entries.found: Blaenavon, Torfaen, Wales
entries.notes: Closed 1980, reopened 1983 as a museum; one of the few mines in the world you can still descend into with original machinery.

entries.name: Cerro Rico (Potosí)
cultures: Spanish colonial; Quechua and Aymara forced labour; today Bolivian cooperatives
entries.purpose: the richest silver deposit in history; financed the Spanish Empire
parts: cone-shaped mountain 4,782 m a.s.l. honeycombed with ~600 mines at peak
hundreds of shafts and adits; ~22 artificial reservoirs for 120 stamp mills
guaira llama-dung furnaces on the slopes
mint (Casa de la Moneda) at the foot
layout: ore followed down dip from the oxidised cap into tin-rich depth
Potosí grew to ~160,000 people by 1650, bigger than London or Amsterdam
mita forced-labour drafts from across the Andes fed the mines
entries.found: Potosí, Bolivia
entries.notes: An estimated 60,000 t (possibly up to 90,000 t) of silver produced; ~80% of the world's silver in the 16th-18th centuries came from here; still mined by cooperatives; UNESCO World Heritage Site.

entries.name: Witwatersrand gold reefs
entries.purpose: the greatest goldfield on Earth
parts: arcuate 350 km basin with ~7 major goldfields
reefs only 1-2 m thick but extraordinarily persistent
Mponeng mine reaches ~4 km deep (world's deepest mine)
heaps of cyanide tailings with measurable radiation
layout: reefs dip south from the outcrop near Johannesburg
main reef mined along strike for 300+ km
cyanidation (1890) made the refractory ore payable and saved the field
entries.found: Gauteng Province, South Africa (Johannesburg sits on the edge of the field)
entries.notes: Roughly 30-40% of all the gold ever mined (~53,000 t) came from these reefs; the Witwatersrand alone is said to hold about half the world's remaining gold resources.

entries.name: Almadén mercury mine
cultures: Roman; Arab; Spanish Crown; Fugger bankers
entries.purpose: the world's largest mercury source; silver depended on it
parts: mines of the Almadén syncline (San Teodoro, Guadalperal, mines in the hill west of town)
Royal forced-labour gaol (the 'mina real' convicts)
on 18th-century furnaces at the mine yard
Almadén Mining Park with tours into the 16th-century mine
layout: cinnabar veins near surface oxidised, mined since Romans for vermilion
post-1555 Medina amalgamation drove demand for American silver
supplied roughly one-third of all mercury ever used
entries.found: Almadén, Ciudad Real, Spain
entries.notes: UNESCO-listed with Idrija (Slovenia). In 1559 the Crown took the monopoly; convict labour killed thousands. Mining ceased 2001, metallurgy 2003, marketing by 2011.

entries.name: Cornish and West Devon tin-copper mines
entries.purpose: tin and copper for the Industrial Revolution; Cornish technology exported worldwide
parts: shafts, adits and lodes in granite (typical mines 300-800 m deep; South Crofty ~800 m)
beam-engine houses pumping water (outstanding industrial architecture)
stamps, buddles and settling pits for ore dressing
Geevor and King Edward Mine: the two near-complete survivors
layout: lodes followed down dip in granite
early 19th c. produced two-thirds of world copper
Cornish miners migrated to Mexico, South Africa, Butte, Lake Superior
entries.found: Cornwall and West Devon, England (UNESCO World Heritage Site 2006)
entries.notes: The landscape is the exhibit: clifftop engine houses (St Agnes), Geevor surface plant, underground tours at King Edward. Last tin mine (South Crofty) closed 1998.

entries.name: Wieliczka salt mine
entries.purpose: 700 years of salt; now a UNESCO-listed underground city and tourist mine
parts: 9 levels, deepest 327 m
over 240 km of galleries and 2,350 chambers
St. Kinga chapel carved entirely from salt (incl. chandeliers)
Daniłowicz shaft visitor descent
layout: deposit 5.5 km long, 0.5-1.5 km wide, salt from 57 m down
rails and horse-gins replaced by tourists since 1978
Brine flooded or pillars left to support the chambers
entries.found: Wieliczka, near Kraków, Poland (with the Bochnia twin mine)
entries.notes: UNESCO since 1978; rock-salt extraction halted 1964, all salt ended 1996; around a million visitors a year descend 380 steps into the mountain.

entries.name: Carrara marble quarries
entries.purpose: the most famous sculptural marble on Earth
parts: 650+ quarries on the Apuan Alps
Fantiscritti, Colonnata and Ravaccione basins
underground 'cathedral' quarries and open amphitheatre faces
white marble 'snow that never melts' visible from the coast
layout: quarry faces follow the bedding of the Apuan limestone
marble railed or trucked to Carrara and Marina di Carrara port
Michelangelo chose his own blocks in person (David, 1501-1504)
entries.found: Apuan Alps, province of Massa-Carrara, Tuscany, Italy
entries.notes: More marble has been quarried here than anywhere else; pure statuario is exhausted; Romans shipped it as 'marmor lunense' for the Pantheon and Trajan's Column.

entries.name: Pentelic marble quarries
entries.purpose: the stone of the Parthenon and the Acropolis
parts: Dionysos quarry (modern) and ancient opencasts on Mt Pentelicus
Davelis Cave, an ancient quarry-chamber
the 'marble road' with slip tracks down to the plain (~16 km)
layout: quarry blocks rolled/dragged 16-20 km downhill to ships at Phaleron
~20,000 tonnes of marble went into the Parthenon alone
today quarried almost only to restore the Acropolis itself
entries.found: Mount Pentelicus, 16 km northeast of Athens, Greece
entries.notes: The only living source of the same stone Phidias used; the modern restoration of the Parthenon is obliged to come from here.

entries.name: Portland stone quarries
entries.purpose: the white-grey freestone that is London's 'own' building stone
parts: Broadcroft, Grove, Nicodemus Knob and Tout quarries
Nicodemus Knob: a single unquarried monolith left behind
Jordan's Mine: underground workings 50+ m below the island
layout: beds of freestone separated by chert partings
stone barged around the coast and up the Thames
Wren took ~1 million cubic feet for St Paul's after the Great Fire
entries.found: Isle of Portland, Dorset, England
entries.notes: St Paul's, the Cenotaph, the British Museum, Buckingham Palace and the UN headquarters in New York are all clad in it; most new Portland stone is now mined underground.

entries.name: Aswan granite quarries (Unfinished Obelisk)
entries.purpose: the source of Egyptian obelisk granite; walked away from the largest one ever attempted
parts: the unfinished obelisk, 41.75 m long, still attached to bedrock
estimated weight ~1,168 tonnes had it been parted and raised
trenches and wedge pits from the work gangs
rock paintings (dolphins, ostriches) by the workers
layout: quarry pit in the Northern Quarries, 1.5 km from Aswan
obelisk abandoned when a crack ran the length of the shaft
other part-finished granite monuments litter the same quarry
entries.found: Northern Quarries, Aswan, Egypt
entries.notes: The single largest stone object the ancients ever tried to move; left in situ since the reign of Hatshepsut; its diorite pounding balls are scattered across the floor.

entries.name: Grimes Graves (Neolithic flint mines)
entries.purpose: the largest known prehistoric flint mine; axes for half of Britain
parts: 433 recorded shafts and pits over ~37 ha, originally more
shafts up to 15 m deep and 4-12 m diameter at the surface
radiating galleries at the bottom following the floorstone seam
backfilled shafts leave a pockmarked moonscape
layout: chalk dug out, flint floorstone prised out from below
shafts backfilled with spoil for stability after digging
axes from this flint reached Devon and Scotland
entries.found: near Brandon, Norfolk, England
entries.notes: One shaft open to visitors down a 9 m ladder. Roughly 16-18,000 tonnes of flint extracted; 2,000 tonnes of chalk had to leave one large shaft before floorstone was reached.

entries.name: Rudna Glava (prehistoric copper mine)
entries.purpose: perhaps the oldest known mine on Earth; the start of European copper
parts: ~40 funnel-shaped shafts, 1-2 m wide, up to 20 m deep
working platforms at the shaft mouths
hoards of pottery and stone mauls left in situ
layout: green oxidised copper veins (malachite, azurite) traced to depth
rock heated then doused, cracked, broken with grooved river-pebble mauls and antler picks
shafts backfilled after digging
entries.found: near Majdanpek, eastern Serbia
entries.notes: Vinča culture miners opened the metal age anywhere in Europe; modern magnetite mining in the 20th century sat directly on top of the prehistoric works.

entries.name: Muzo emerald mine
cultures: Muzo indigenous; Spanish; Colombian state; Muzo International
materials: or 'black shales' of the Paja Formation
entries.purpose: the source of the world's finest emeralds
parts: underground galleries: Tequendama, Catedral, Puerto Arturo, La Rampa (~400 m deep)
emeralds grown in hydrothermal veins 30-40 million years ago
trapiche emeralds (star-spoke inclusions) found nowhere else
layout: veins followed by tunnelling with hand tools in the green war years
Fura (2.2 kg, ~11,000 carats) and Tena (400 g) found here in 1999
the miners' peace accord of 1990 ended the 'green wars'
entries.found: Boyacá, 100 km north of Bogotá, Colombia
entries.notes: Worked by the Muzo people before the Spanish arrived (rediscovered 1559); the quality benchmark for trapiche and fine green stones; the Devonshire emerald (1,384 carats) is the most famous single stone.

entries.name: Argyle diamond mine
cultures: Australian (Rio Tinto); Miriwoong, Gija, Malgnin, Wularr traditional owners
materials: open pit then underground block cave (2013)
entries.purpose: the world's main source of pink diamonds; the largest natural coloured-diamond mine
parts: single lamproite pipe ~1.5 km diameter at surface
open pit 1985-2013, underground 2013-2020
two massive tailings 'Pareto' dumps
layout: pipe discovered 1979 by a mineral prospector on foot, not by drilling
alluvial mining first (1983), open pit (1985), underground (2013)
AK1 pipe carried pink, red, violet, champagne and cognac stones
entries.found: East Kimberley region, Western Australia
entries.notes: Produced ~865 million carats and over 90% of the world's pink diamonds; closed 3 November 2020; now being rehabilitated to hand back to Traditional Owners.

entries.name: Berkeley Pit
entries.purpose: open-pit copper mine, now America's most toxic lake
parts: pit 1.6 km by 0.8 km, max depth 540 m
~270 m of water at pH 2.5-4.5, heavy-metal laden
~10,000 miles of underground mine workings beneath Butte
layout: dewatering pumps stopped in 1982; pit is now a groundwater sump
in November 2016 an estimated 4,000 snow geese landed and died
horseshoe bend water treatment plant pumps out since 2019
entries.found: Butte, Montana, USA
entries.notes: EPA Superfund since 1987; pit water must never reach the protective level of 5,410 ft above sea level or it would drain into Silver Bow Creek; mining stopped for good.

entries.name: Giant Mine
entries.purpose: gold mine; now an underground waste tomb being frozen forever
parts: 237,000 tonnes of arsenic trioxide dust stored in 14 underground chambers
frozen-block method: thermosyphons will keep chambers at -5 C indefinitely
remediation scheduled to 2038
layout: roasting the ore to liberate gold released arsenic gas
dust collected and bagged underground since the 1950s
Yellowknife sits ~5 km from the chambers; the waste must never thaw
entries.found: Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, Canada
entries.notes: Roasting arsenopyrite to free gold killed workers and poisoned the region; the chambers hold ~79% arsenic trioxide dust and are Canada's most expensive environmental liability.

entries.name: Whitby jet mines
materials: fossilised Araucaria wood (Upper Lias Jet Rock)
entries.purpose: the black 'gemstone' of Victorian mourning jewellery
parts: drift mines driven into the cliffs (Ravenscar to Saltburn) and inland (North York Moors)
~300 recorded mines; narrow 1 m by 1.8 m passages
red spoil-tips along the contour mark the drift lines
layout: jet in isolated nodules, not seams: mining was treasure-hunting
cliff mines on suspended timber platforms at low tide
Whitby: 200+ workshops, 1,500 workers at the 1870s peak
entries.found: Whitby and North York Moors, England
entries.notes: Queen Victoria wore jet after Prince Albert died in 1861; the fashion collapsed after WWI; no new jet mining rights granted since the early 1900s.
